rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Near the Day of Judgement Gog and Magog will erupt from every side, filling the world with disorder; only God knows exactly how this will happen.
rows.anchor: near the Day of Judgement, Gog and Magog will launch an onslaught from all sides and the whole world will be filled with disorder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their mention tells Muhammad not to spend more time on sign-demanding rejecters: Qur'anic arguments from nature and intellect will not persuade them, and belief at the imminent Judgment will be useless.
rows.anchor: they will only accept faith when the Day of Judgement will stare them in the eye

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People consider the Judgment far away, but it is near by God's measure; humans judge time by their short standards, unlike God.
rows.anchor: they regard it to be far off, and We see it very near at hand

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Judgment's sudden arrival will horrify those who demanded it and mocked it, leaving them staring in fear and consternation.
rows.anchor: will be struck with fear and consternation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The confession begins with an omitted speech verb; disbelievers admit that messengers tried to awaken them, yet they wronged themselves and mocked the warnings.
rows.anchor: God did send people for this purpose who did their utmost to awaken them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The obstacle to belief is indifference, not a lack of evidence: the Judgment conflicts with people's desires, so they defer preparation until it arrives.
rows.anchor: the real impediment is the indifference of people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The confession will not help: whether they plead or cry, idolaters must enter Hell, with no escape from its destructive pit.
rows.anchor: whether they plead or cry, they will have to encounter the destructive pit of Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The letter mā refers to the idols and stones worshipped by the idolaters; using mā for nonliving things is common.
rows.anchor: indicates that they refer to the idols and stones the Idolaters used to worship.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making the idols fuel for Hell is not to punish the idols; it displays their terrible fate to the people who worshipped them.
rows.anchor: The purpose of making these idols into the fuel of Hell is obviously not to punish them;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lāt, Manāt, ʿUzzā, and Ḥabl were invented, hypothetical names without real existence.
rows.anchor: were mere hypothetical names that they had invented and did not exist in reality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idolaters worshipped those imagined deities as stone idols.
rows.anchor: they would worship them in the form of stone idols.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fate of nations that worshipped prophets and righteous people is discussed elsewhere; Jesus's testimony against Christian worshippers appears in Sūrah al-Māʾidah.
rows.anchor: The fate of some polytheistic nations who used to worship prophets and righteous individuals is not mentioned here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets and righteous people will disavow their worshippers, say they did not know they were worshipped, and insist they never commanded such worship.
rows.anchor: they never told them to worship them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols' entry into Hell humiliates worshippers who had relied on them, showing both worshippers and deities helpless and punished.
rows.anchor: This would be extreme humiliation for those who were the last hope of all their desires.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worshippers and the worshipped will remain together in Hell eternally.
rows.anchor: both the worshippers and the worshipped will eternally remain together in Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first part of the verse directly addresses the idolaters, while the second declares their permanent fate.
rows.anchor: the first part of this verse will be directly addressed to them and the second one is a declaration of their permanent fate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word zaf means pleading and crying.
rows.anchor: The word زَﻓmeans “pleadings and crying.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first pronoun refers to the worshippers and the second to the idols; their antecedents are definite, so the shift is not an ambiguity but gives brevity.
rows.anchor: in the first sentence is for the worshippers and in the second for the idols.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worshippers plead in Hell while their stone idols neither hear them nor know they were worshipped, despite the worshippers' belief in them.
rows.anchor: the mere stones they regarded as deities and worshipped will not even know that they were being worshipped and sought help from.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other Qur'anic passages portray Hell's inhabitants imploring for help with no one there to help them.
rows.anchor: the companions of Hell will implore for help but none will be there to help them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The living-being verb and pronoun can refer to stones by adopting the worshippers' own belief that idols hear their pleas, a usage found in classical Arabic and the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: they are used with reference to the opinion of the worshippers: they considered these stones to hear their pleadings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun qualified by the verb 'kept away' is suppressed; the verse means that those promised a good fate by God will be kept away from Hell.
rows.anchor: those who have already been promised a good fate by God will be kept away from Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of this good fate was stated earlier: whoever does righteous deeds with faith will not have their effort wasted.
rows.anchor: The promise of this good fate has been mentioned earlier in verse 94.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the view that 19:71 means everyone, believers included, must pass over Hell; it arises from misidentifying the address in that verse.
rows.anchor: This verse clearly refutes the opinion of those people who,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If people cannot adapt the luxuries around them, monotony will bore them and make them desire new surroundings for entertainment.
rows.anchor: If a person does not have the freedom to alter and adapt the luxuries provided to him,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans prefer bliss on their own terms, so Paradise grants believers the variety they desire without hindrance, beyond any earthly emperor; al-Kahf says its companions would not wish to leave.
rows.anchor: If a person does not have the freedom to alter and adapt the luxuries provided to him,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised day is the great upheaval of the whole universe when the trumpet is blown.
rows.anchor: the great upheaval that will take place in the whole universe once the trumpet is blown.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an depicts this upheaval in many places, especially in the final sūrahs; 21:97's image of disbelievers staring suddenly points to it.
rows.anchor: The words “then all of a sudden those who have disbelieved will stare in astonishment” of verse 97 are pointing towards it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-sijill means a scroll or register in which written pages are preserved.
rows.anchor: refers to the scroll or register in which written pages are preserved.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word kutub here means written pages.
rows.anchor: here means “written pages” and

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author parses the phrase about the first creation grammatically as a locus in the description of creation anew.
rows.anchor: The way We began the first creation, in the same way, We shall do it again.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression meaning 'for the first time' occurs in other Qur'anic passages with the same sense.
rows.anchor: is also used in the Qur’ān at various instances to convey this meaning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The participle in 'a promise upon Us' emphasizes that the promise is certain, as earlier wording also indicates.
rows.anchor: is for emphasis, ie it is a certain promise from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's words that He is certain to do it mean the promise is no bluff: He has decreed it and its fulfillment is easy for Him.
rows.anchor: The words “indeed, We are certain to do it” imply that no one should think that they are being sounded a bluff.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refers to the Psalms, whose chapter 37 focuses especially on the earth being inherited by God's righteous servants.
rows.anchor: This verse refers to the Psalms.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Psalm 37 is especially devoted to the promise that God's righteous servants inherit the earth, supporting the Qur'an's reference.
rows.anchor: dedicated to this one fact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reproduces Psalm 37 in full to show which 'earth' the verse means and clarify its allusion and wording.
rows.anchor: becomes clear which “earth” is being referred to here.

rows.speaker: Psalms
rows.claim: Psalm 37 contrasts the wicked, who wither and are destroyed, with those who trust in the Lord and inherit the land; the meek enjoy peace there.
rows.anchor: those who are evil will be destroyed

rows.speaker: Psalms
rows.claim: Psalm 37 reiterates that the righteous inherit and dwell in the land forever, God protects the faithful, and the wicked and their offspring perish.
rows.anchor: righteous will inherit the land
